analytic.title: Research on Xen Virtualization and Scheduling Algorithm Based on Mixed-criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper analyzes the real-time guarantee problem and CPU resource allocation problem of Xen scheduling in mixed criticality systems, and proposes a virtual machine scheduling idea for Xen mixed-criticality systems. By adjusting VCPU resources under different load conditions, the CPU resources occupied by non-real-time virtual machines are reasonably allocated while ensuring real-time performance. In view of the passive treatment of low-criticality tasks in mixed criticality systems, a preemptive mixed criticality task global scheduling method SWPA is proposed. The algorithm is based on a dynamic weight adjustment factor, combined with the criticality and time sensitivity of the task, dynamically evaluates the importance of the task, and assigns priority to the task. The correctness of the method is proved by theoretical deduction. Simulation experiments show that this method is superior to the existing classic scheduling algorithms EDF-DVD and Credit in terms of the schedulability of low-criticality tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Virtualization technology enables functional partitioning of multi-core embedded systems, allowing applications with different criticality levels to run on a single platform. This consolidation reduces costs, power consumption, and space utilization while improving reliability and security through isolation between different operating systems [1]. However, challenges remain, such as the uncertain performance of ARM v8 virtualization extensions in onboard systems, and whether virtualization exacerbates performance jitter, particularly in airborne systems with strict real-time requirements. Current solutions like Wind River® Helix™ are expensive and closed-source, hindering the development of the aerospace ecosystem [2]. In contrast, open-source hypervisors like KVM and Xen, and embedded-specific solutions like Jailhouse and Xvisor, offer more flexible options. Mixed-criticality systems, common in sectors like aerospace, require isolation between high-and low-criticality tasks, with lightweight virtualization ensuring that noncritical tasks do not affect the performance of critical ones [3]. In such systems, effective resource allocation between realtime and non-real-time operating systems is crucial to maintaining real-time performance. This paper proposes a hierarchical scheduling idea for virtual machines in Xen's mixed-criticality system. By adjusting VCPU resources under different load conditions, the CPU resources occupied by non-real-time virtual machines are reasonably allocated under the condition of ensuring real-time performance. In view of the passive treatment of low-criticality tasks in mixed-criticality systems, a preemptive mixed-criticality task global scheduling method is proposed. Based on the dynamic weight adjustment factor, the algorithm combines the criticality and time sensitivity of the task to dynamically evaluate the importance of the task and assign priorities to the task. The correctness of the method is proved through theoretical derivation.

div.head: A. Xen Virtualization
div.p: Xen is an open source Type-1 hypervisor. [4] It is currently applied in a variety of commercial and open source projects, including embedded devices, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), desktop virtualization, and server virtualization. In Xen, client operating systems are called domains. Domain 0 (Dom0) is a privileged domain through which Xen manages other non-privileged domains (DomU).

div.head: B. Optimization work
div.p: Mixed criticality systems need to support both highpriority real-time tasks and low-priority non-real-time tasks. In the Xen platform, virtual machines share underlying physical resources (PCPU) through VCPU abstraction. Although existing scheduling algorithms (such as Credit2) perform well in non-real-time environments, they cannot effectively meet the scheduling requirements of real-time tasks when real-time and non-real-time tasks coexist, and it is difficult to fully utilize the remaining resources. Therefore, it is critical to design a hierarchical scheduling mechanism for real-time guarantee and resource optimization [5]. Toumassian et al. (2016) studied the performance overhead of Xen on the ARM architecture and compared it with Jailhouse and native Linux systems. The results show that although Xen has a higher overhead than Jailhouse, the real-time and predictability of the system can be significantly improved by adopting a real-time scheduler (RTDS) instead of the default Credit scheduler. In addition, studies have shown that Xen exhibits greater flexibility in scenarios with higher demands for dynamic resource allocation, but this flexibility comes at the expense of increased performance overhead [6]. Schulz and Annighöfer (2022) analyzed the suitability of Xen for real-time safety-critical applications. Through experiments based on Intel architecture, the study revealed two major limitations of Xen: First, cache conflicts between virtual machines may cause temporal isolation problems, although this problem can be solved by cache coloring techniques (such as the method proposed by Ye et al., 2014). ) is partially solved; secondly, the Xen code size is large, especially the Intel x86 version, which may pose a challenge to the system authentication process. Despite this, the research believes that Xen still has certain potential in realtime application scenarios [7].

To further optimize the real-time performance of Xen, McFarland and Awad (2022) proposed an alternative scheduler -Trasspose Xen. The scheduler analyzes the impact of multiple resource sharing (including PCPU, LLC and memory) between virtual machines on the worst case execution time (WCET), introduces virtual deadline and EDF-based scheduling mechanism, and thus achieves hard real-time constraints. Experimental results show that compared with classic Xen schedulers (RTDS and Credit), Trasspose Xen can significantly reduce latency and effectively avoid starvation of non-real-time virtual machines [8].

div.head: C. Hierarchical Scheduling Idea
div.p:  Adopting the hierarchical concept: DomU running on Xen is divided into real-time and non-real-time categories. Real-time DomU uses the preemptive SWPA algorithm, and non-real-time tasks use the Credit algorithm.

 Real-time DomUs are assigned fixed VCPUs to undertake critical tasks. The load of these VCPUs is monitored in real time to ensure that they can complete their tasks on time; non-real-time DomUs will not use these fixed VCPUs initially, but when the real-time VCPU load is low, the system will dynamically adjust and allow non-real-time DomUs to temporarily use these VCPU resources, thereby improving the resource utilization of the overall system.
 Introduce load monitoring and early warning mechanisms to quickly adjust resource allocation and ensure priority execution of real-time tasks.

 Load monitoring mechanism implementation: mainly through the collection of VCPU usage, task waiting queue length and execution delay and other key performance indicators. The system regularly collects and analyzes these data. If it is found that the usage of some VCPUs exceeds the preset threshold or the task queue time is too long, the system will dynamically adjust the resource allocation strategy and prioritize the allocation of resources to the realtime DomU to ensure that its key tasks are not affected.

div.head: III. SWPA ALGORITHM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: In mixed criticality systems, the criticality and execution time of tasks may change as the system operating state changes (e.g., switching from low criticality to high criticality). The Sensitivity Weight Priority Algorithm (SWPA) is a simple and efficient algorithm focused on dynamic scheduling of tasks, suitable for real-time task management in mixed criticality systems and virtualization platforms. The algorithm dynamically evaluates the importance of tasks and assigns priorities to tasks based on dynamic weight adjustment factors, combined with the criticality and time sensitivity of tasks.

div.head: A. Mission Model
div.p: Mixed criticality systems contain a finite number of independent periodic tasks 𝛤 = {𝜏 1 , 𝜏 2 ⋯ , 𝜏 𝑛 }, that is, each task can be represented by a four-tuple 𝜏 𝑖 = (𝑇 𝑖 , 𝐷 𝑖 , 𝐿 𝑖 , 𝐶 𝑖 ), where:
 𝑇 𝑖 ∈ 𝑁 + is the task cycle, which indicates the minimum time interval between any two adjacent jobs in the task 𝜏 𝑖 .
 𝐷 𝑖 ∈ 𝑁 + is the relative deadline of the task τ i , which indicates the maximum allowed response time of each job released by the task τ i . The implicit deadline is used, that is 𝐷 𝑖 = 𝑇 𝑖 .
 𝐿 𝑖 ∈ {1,2, ⋯ , 𝑙}indicates the critical level of the task τ i . The larger the value, the higher the critical level.

Where represents the maximum critical level in the mixed critical system. To facilitate subsequent research, this paper studies the mixed critical system with only dual critical levels (𝑙 = 2), and uses 𝐿𝑂 to represent the low critical level and 𝐻𝐼 to represent the high critical level.

 𝐶 𝑖 ∈ (𝐶 𝑖 (1), 𝐶 𝑖 (2), ⋯ , 𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘)) is a 𝑘 -dimensional vector, corresponding to the worst execution time WCET of the task at different critical levels.𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘)satisfies the following two properties: 1) 𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘) is monotonically non-decreasing with 𝑘 . If 𝑘 1 ≤ 𝑘 2 , then 𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘 1 ) ≤ 𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘 2 ) . 2) When 𝑘 ≥ 𝐿 𝑖 , 𝐶 𝑖 (𝑘) = 𝐶 𝑖 (𝐿 𝑖 ). That is, when the criticality of the system exceeds the criticality of the job itself, the WCET of the job no longer increases with the increase of the criticality of the system.

div.head: B. Job Model
div.p: An execution of a mixed-criticality task 𝜏 𝑖 is called a job, and the job sequence in each task 𝜏 𝑖 is infinite and released periodically. A mixed-criticality job can be represented by a four-tuple 𝐽 𝑖 = (𝑟 𝑖 , 𝑑 𝑖 , 𝑡 𝑖 , 𝑥 𝑖 , 𝑐 𝑖 ), where:  𝑟 𝑖 represents the time when the job is released, at which the job can start to execute;

 𝑑 𝑖 represents the absolute deadline of the job. The job is required to be completed before this time. Its value is the sum of the job release time and the relative deadline time, that is 𝑑 𝑖 = 𝑟 𝑖 + 𝐷 𝑖 ;

 𝑥 𝑖 represents the criticality level of the job, which is consistent with the corresponding task criticality level. The larger its value, the higher the criticality level. In this paper, the value 𝑥 𝑖 is limited to 1 (low) or 2 (high);

 𝑐 𝑖 represents a two-dimensional vector group, that is 𝑐 𝑖 [𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂), 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼)] , where 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂) represents the worst execution time of the job 𝐽 𝑖 when the criticality level is 𝐿𝑂 , and 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼) represents the worst execution time of the job 𝐽 𝑖 when the criticality level is 𝐻𝑂.

div.head: D. Algorithm ideas
div.p: The algorithm flow is shown in Figure 1. 2) According to the definition, the various parameter values of the task are calculated, and the values of the comprehensive impact factors corresponding to the task at different critical levels are calculated and stored.

3) Priority is determined and sorted according to the comprehensive impact factors of the tasks, and then they are added to the ready queue (initially sorted according to the task priority at the LO level). 4) Schedule tasks in the ready queue.

When a task at level HI exceeds the worst execution corresponding to the current critical level during execution, the system raises the critical level, reorders the tasks in the ready queue (at level HI), and then continues execution.

div.head: E. Algorithm Implementation
div.p: 1) Before scheduling begins, the system is initialized, the current criticality level is set to low, and the priority of each task is calculated. The high-priority task is added to the ready queue, and this process is repeated until all tasks are added to the queue.

div.head: Scheduling Strategy
div.p: Input：Task Set 𝝉 Output：The scheduling sequence of 1 2) The main process of scheduling is as follows: Schedule tasks in order of priority in the ready queue. During operation, monitor the system criticality status in real time. If the criticality does not increase, continue to execute tasks until all tasks are completed or the specified time is reached; if the criticality increases, switch the system criticality to high, recalculate the criticality parameters of the tasks in the ready queue, and continue scheduling after reordering according to the new priority. Under the current criticality, the execution of high-criticality tasks is prioritized, and lowcriticality tasks are scheduled only when they do not affect high-criticality tasks.

div.head: System criticality Key Parameter Calculation Results
A. Simulation experiment verification and analysis
div.p: This experiment mainly involves the generation of four parameters, namely the worst execution time under high and low criticality levels 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼), 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂) , the period 𝑇 𝑖 (the default period is equal to the deadline) and the system criticality 𝑘. Task generation is randomly generated according to the method in the literature [9], as follows:
 The task utilization 𝑈 𝑖 is generated using the UUnifast algorithm. Since the test platform is a 4core processor, its value is between [1.2, 3.6] and obeys a uniform distribution [10].
 The period 𝑇 𝑖 is randomly generated in the range of (10, 50) ms, and 𝐷 𝑖 = 𝑇 𝑖 .
 The execution time at low criticality 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂) is set based on utilization and cycle time, 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂) = 𝑈 𝑖 • 𝑇 𝑖 .

 The value of 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼)is determined according to the critical level of the task. When k = 1 , 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂) = 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼), When k = 2, 𝑐 𝑖 (𝐻𝐼) = 𝛼𝑐 𝑖 (𝐿𝑂), where α ∈ (1.2,1.5), and the probability of generating a task with a high critical level is 0.4.

For each utilization rate, 10 task sets are randomly generated, each containing 10 tasks. To minimize the possible errors during operation, each task set contains at least 1,000 job instances. The final results are compared by calculating the average of the running results of the 10 task sets under the utilization rate.

div.head: B. Experimental results analysis
div.p: In order to verify the effectiveness of the algorithm, the Credit algorithm and EDF-DVD algorithm were selected for experimental comparison with the SWPA algorithm. Credit in terms of schedulability of low-criticality tasks.

To facilitate experimental verification, the hybrid critical tasks in the hybrid critical system studied in this paper are for dual critical levels. In actual systems, there will also be multiple (k > 2) critical levels. For systems with multiple critical levels, the switching of system critical levels will be more frequent, which will also make the task execution process more complicated. In the future, we will conduct an in-depth analysis of the impact of system critical level switching on the task execution process and explore feasible solutions.

div.p: It can be observed from Figure 2 that the SWPA algorithm outperforms the other two algorithms in terms of overall task schedulability. The original intention of the Credit algorithm was to allocate resources based on fairness rather than focusing on the scheduling of real-time tasks. As task utilization increases, resource competition intensifies. Especially when resource utilization reaches 0.7, highpriority real-time tasks may not be scheduled in time, resulting in a decrease in schedulability. EDF-DVD is based on the EDF-VD algorithm, which can better balance the realtime performance and resource utilization of tasks. However, when the average resource utilization exceeds 0.75, the virtual deadline adjustment strategy may cause lowcriticality tasks to be postponed or even discarded, which in turn causes scheduling performance degradation. The SWPA algorithm introduces an adjustment factor and a dynamic evaluation mechanism of the idle window in the priority calculation to ensure that high-criticality tasks maintain higher priorities at different criticality levels, and at the same time, the idle window between the worst execution time and the deadline of the task is adjusted. Window, reasonably schedule low-criticality tasks. This mechanism significantly improves the overall schedulability of tasks, effectively avoiding task losses and maximizing the utilization efficiency of system resources even under high utilization. Figure 3 shows the deadline miss rate (DMR) of lowcriticality tasks. Figure 4 shows the high-criticality tasks. SWPA outperforms other algorithms in the acceptance rate of low-criticality tasks because it introduces the idle time window of tasks in its priority calculation. This ensures that low-criticality tasks with earlier deadlines can be scheduled as soon as possible after the high-criticality tasks are completed.

For EDF-DVD and Credit algorithms, due to the restriction on task utilization, the task loss rate of the former increases significantly when the normalized resource utilization reaches 0.75; while the latter, although the Credit algorithm focuses on fairness in scheduling, it has a negative impact on high-criticality tasks. Prioritizing low-criticality tasks may result in low-criticality tasks not being executed in a timely manner under high load conditions. This is because the credit allocation of tasks depends on the availability of resources, and high-criticality tasks may occupy more resources, causing scheduling delays for low-criticality tasks. When system resources are tight, the fairness of the Credit algorithm may cause low-criticality tasks to be "delayed" in execution, especially under high load or high utilization conditions, which increases the deadline miss rate of lowcriticality tasks. In contrast, in the DMR indicator of highcriticality tasks, the SWPA algorithm shows excellent performance, and its high-criticality task loss rate is almost 0, which fully proves the effectiveness and reliability of the algorithm in ensuring the real-time performance of highcriticality tasks. div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: The concept of mixed-criticality system has been proposed for more than ten years, and there are abundant relevant research results. This paper proposes new improvement ideas for the problems and shortcomings of Xen in mixed-criticality system tasks and verifies them. The main contents of this paper are as follows:

1) This paper analyzes the real-time guarantee problem and CPU resource allocation problem of Xen scheduling in mixed-criticality systems, and proposes a virtual machine scheduling idea for Xen's mixed-criticality systems. By adjusting VCPU resources under different load conditions, the CPU resources occupied by non-real-time virtual machines are reasonably allocated while ensuring real-time performance.

2) Aiming at the problem of low schedulability of lowcriticality tasks in mixed-criticality task scheduling, a preemptive mixed-criticality task global scheduling method SWPA is proposed. The algorithm is based on dynamic weight adjustment factors, combined with the criticality and time sensitivity of tasks, dynamically evaluates the importance of tasks, and assigns priorities to tasks.
